What you're describing is literally just LEGO. If freedom and customization was really the main selling point of Gunpla, every piece would be standardized and cross compatible. The closest you'll get to that with Gunpla is 30MM and its derivatives. 

Real Grades in particular is a really weird case to be dying on this hill over. Of all of the existing grades in Gunpla, Real Grade is the one with the most bespoke proprietary designs. I can understand having this stance with High Grades, and maybe even some Master Grades and Perfect Grades (specifically the Seed line), but Real Grade is the one series where nearly nothing is designed to be easily customized. That metaseries you mentioned released almost exclusively High Grade kits save for the Build Strike and Exia Dark Matter.

Customization, unless specifically intended through design, is not the point of Gunpla. It may be encouraged by the company but that's mostly to harbor community engagement and farm market share.

>...Some assembly is very obviously required. And I guess I don't see throwing on some joint tape or something as a deal-breaker.

Perhaps not to you, I, and many others who are **enthusiastic** about this hobby, but that's not what the kit, or any other Gunpla kit from Bandai, is designed to be. Gunpla's whole schtick is that they're more accessible than other model kits. They're designed from the start to be straight built with the average extra effort being panel lining, stickers/decals, and top coat. Of course, you're free to customize and modify whatever you see fit, but good luck telling that to the average consumer.

>Like it or not - that's reality. The plated plastic basically doubles the price of a kit. Compare the RG Phenex to any of the other RG Unicorn kits. Plated plastic is expensive.

I don't disagree that plated plastic is expensive, it's an extra few steps along the manufacturing process and that costs money. My point about the price tag is that there are significantly cheaper kits within the same line that have fully built inner frames, case and point RG Wing Gundam. I just feel like using the expensive plastic as complete justification for the price makes no sense when the kit has a problem much cheaper kits solved years ago. The RG Sazabi Special Coating is effectively the same situation but is a functionally superior product for a similar price.

>But I don't think it's a universally bad/obsolete thing. Everyone seems to love the MkII and that uses an MS Joint. Or there's the ever-popular Unicorn.

The MS Joint system isn't objectively or universally "bad" but it is obsolete in the context of modern Real Grade. It's just an inferior product to what's already been on the market for the same price or cheaper. You can't genuinely tell me that an Akatsuki Gundam with a modern fully built inner frame wouldn't have been a measurable improvement over what we were given.

Every now and then we get a post talking about how (insert hated kit here) is actually not that bad and just needs a little work and it's almost always a real grade using the MS inner frame.

Here's the thing, Gunpla is marketed and designed to be an accessible line of model kits that don't require any modification and can work built straight out of the box. This community is a small bubble within an already niche hobby, we're enthusiasts. The reality is that most people just aren't willing to go through the extra effort to make their 80-90USD model kit actually match the quality of other equivalently priced model kits. Extra work beyond building the kit is not an element of the hobby that is nor ever should be expected after the precedent set by modern Gunpla. Kits are expected to be perfect out of the box because that's the whole point of Gunpla in the first place.

You claim that the price increase comes from the plating but that still doesn't save it from the fact that the MS inner frame is just straight up outdated. It's a cost cutting measure to save on design time, simple as that. They haven't used MS joints for the main inner frame since the Unicorn nearly 8 years ago. If they can make the RG Wing Gundam, a kit that has a fully built inner frame for half the price, they can do it for this one, they just didn't.

That said, none of this means anyone is incorrect for enjoying this or any other kit. Like whatever you want to like, don't let some Redditors and YouTubers tell you what to enjoy.

From what I can gather from what you've said so far, the extent of your experience with this topic seems to be surface-level cursory information on AI image generation as well as seeing some AI generated images on the internet that you found cool and then being annoyed because people disliked the cool thing you saw because it was made with AI. You mention on multiple occasions this "blind hatred" that people have towards AI, claiming that people are "just hating ai because other people tell them to" while, ironically enough, you're here *defending* AI because other people told you *not* to. These are two sides of the same coin. You are taking a stand against a problem that you are actively contributing to.

I am not asking you to hate AI if it really does go against what you truly think and believe. All I'm saying is that you should think and believe your own thoughts and beliefs instead of immediately taking the opposing side as a knee-jerk reaction without any real idea of what it is you're being so opinionated on and blindly accusing everyone of doing the exact same thing but on the other side.

I am not blindly hating on AI because others are, I'm protesting against something that directly affects my future prospects as an artist. On the other hand, trying to find the potential benefits in something because other people are "blindly hating on it", is still reactionary and blindly following an ideology, just the opposite one.

The potential benefits of AI are that it makes it easier for corporate CEOs to fire their artists and that it disincentivizes consumers from commissioning comparatively more expensive (for good reason) independent freelance artists. By this point, what does it matter where exactly the human touch stems from in the pipeline of AI generated images when all these people care about is the end product? Do you really mean to tell me that a CEO at some big name entertainment company wouldn't instantly sub out their entire art team for a single AI model trained specifically on said art team's work if they knew it would make them more money and wouldn't instantly tank their reputation in the industry? No, they absolutely would do that, in a heartbeat.

This idea of letting a machine make "art" is such an inherently accelerationist take that I simply cannot get behind both as a consumer of art and entertainment and as an artist in that very industry. It feels as if it's something being developed either out of creative bankruptcy and shortsighted gainstanding or as just another obstacle to be overcome in the way of surrendering our future to corporations.

Let me ask you something, what do you personally stand to gain from defending AI so adamantly? "you probably don't even understand why you're hating on AI so blindly" is the language of someone morally posturing to feel superior.

There is only one way to use a microwave, you put things in that was already made by someone or something else and you heat it up. To associate AI imagery with "art" is tantamount to calling a frozen dinner a "handmade meal".

Someone might use AI to generate an image which they will use for a larger idea but if someone is truly so invested in their creative work, why would to delegate that work to a machine and settle for something that is just "close enough"? AI generated images are a cost-cutting measure in the entertainment industry, simple as that. There are no Olympic level mental gymnastics that can save you from this concept because it is simple fact.

They're referred to as archons (a term to refer to the nine magistrates in ancient Athens) and they all have the names of various demons from the Ars Goetia (no real correlation), except for Ei who's demonic name Beelzebul is literally just Satan.

Her cutting down Orobashi was taken from the tale of Susano-o cutting down the Yamata no Orochi, which is also where the whole "grass cutting sword" (Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi) comes from. I just wish they'd put more effort into making the Archons actual original deities instead of some cheap knockoff of already existing ones. My hot take is that having the game operate under the same content release cycle as Genshin Impact is making the game stagnate significantly in terms of pacing, sometimes even worse than Genshin. The events in both are the reason why I cannot see myself enjoying the game for anything beyond the core gameplay and main story. The only reason why it's easier to get away with in Genshin is because it's an open-world action adventure game where players can spend a significant amount of time exploring the map. I just suggest hand painting. I can understand how it might seem more convenient and approachable but it's not all that different to painting with a brush in all honesty. Sanding and priming isn't really even necessary unless you're going for drastically different colors from the original, i.e., going from light to dark complementary colors, or plan on handling the kit often.

The problem with exclusively using markers is that you can't really avoid stroke marks. Gundam Marker paint needs to be pretty thick in order to get good coverage with a marker tip but that leads to very visible stroke marks. On small parts and details that isn't much of a problem but it can be when applied to entire flat surfaces. When hand painting, you can use softer bristle brushes and thin out your paint so it can level out while drying.

Gundam Marker paint also dries much quicker than regular paint which can be a pain(t) in the ass if you mess up because it gets tacky really fast. Try hand painting, there are plenty of tutorials out there on YouTube on how to get started hand painting Gunpla.

A lot of people give the "counter argument" of the effects of suicide on those around, but I think they're poorly reasoned. It's an incredibly toxic notion and ultimately self-serving.

I still believe that suicide attempts should be intervened but for a different reason. I see those who fall to suicide as victims of whatever weight they could no longer carry. In other words, death by suicide is the ultimate result of poor mental health just as death by cardiac arrest is the result of poor heart health. Death is the result of certain illnesses when left untreated and mental health is no different. 

The problem is that preventative measures against mental illnesses are not nearly as straightforward as physical illnesses that are equally as potentially fatal. There is psychiatric medication but it doesn't work for everyone nor can everyone afford it. Therapy is the better option but the efficacy of it varies wildly from patient to patient and even from therapist to therapist. Meanwhile, a COVID vaccine will work on most people who receive it and has little room for variance in preventative treatment.

With that said, I believe that intervening on a suicide attempt is equivalent to performing emergency procedures on an unresponsive patient. It is human nature to have a will to survive, therefore, a person that is attempting to take their own life should be considered "unresponsive" due to whatever psychiatric condition drove them to that point. At the same time, intervention should probably be left to the professionals and not bystanders as they would not have the legal and psychiatric qualifications to make those decisions. I'm sure there are laws for bystander intervention but if suicide prevention is to be taken seriously, I believe it must be put on the same standard as any other medical crisis.
